title: The Late Vow
premise: For ten years, unsigned letters have arrived at Vesper Fairweather's bookshop on the first of every month — apologies, confessions, and one recurring promise: 'When I come back, I'll say what I should have said.' She built a life around their absence: a daughter, a shop, and a careful engagement to Mayor Aldous Crane, whose grip on the town grows darker by the season. When the letters' author, Elias Thorne, buys the house next door, his long-rehearsed sentence collides with her wedding date — and with evidence that Aldous's prosperity was bought with the ruin of families like hers. To speak the vow, Elias must first help Vesper expose the man who owns half the town, and together they learn that belonging isn't granted by power but chosen in defiance of it.
about_author: Felix Okafor is a former small-town bookseller who writes love stories about people who arrive too late and stay anyway. He lives near a river with too many unread letters and one very opinionated cat.

chapters.title: The First of the Month
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. On the morning of another letter's arrival, Vesper balances invoices, her daughter Juniper's school play, and Aldous's announcement of their engagement in the town paper. The emotional beat is quiet resignation — she has stopped hoping the letters will ever name their sender.

chapters.title: A Moving Truck at Number Nine
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias arrives with ten years of unsent drafts and one rehearsed sentence, renting the house beside the bookshop he's loved since before he left. Seeing Vesper through her window, he loses his nerve. The beat is terror disguised as patience.

chapters.title: Recommendations
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. A customer collision over a single copy of a rare poetry collection forces introductions. Vesper feels an unsettling familiarity in Elias's phrasing; Elias recognizes the pressed flower she still keeps in the register. The beat is recognition almost grasped, then lost.

chapters.title: What the Mayor Owns
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias, a land surveyor by trade, is hired by the council and discovers discrepancies in Aldous's development plans — parcels seized from delinquent owners, including the Fairweather family's old orchard. The beat is dread hardening into purpose.

chapters.title: Juniper's Question
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Sharp-eyed Juniper asks why Mr. Thorne looks at Mama like the letters read themselves. Vesper rereads a decade of correspondence and matches a phrase to something Elias said days ago. The beat is vertigo — the answer was next door all along.

chapters.title: The Confrontation at the Orchard
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Vesper confronts Elias among the dead apple trees; he confesses everything — why he left, why the unsigned letters, why he couldn't say the sentence. She slaps the letters against his chest and walks away. The beat is fury that is indistinguishable from heartbreak.

chapters.title: Crane's Offer
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Aldous, sensing a rival, offers Elias a partnership and the surveyor's silence in exchange for leaving town before the wedding. He hints he knows about the letters. Elias refuses, and understands the cost will be paid by Vesper. The beat is temptation refused at a price.

chapters.title: Rehearsal for a Wedding
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Fitting her wedding dress, Vesper finds Aldous's ledger copies missing from the shop safe and realizes he's been watching her. Juniper slips her the orchard deed Elias quietly refiled in her name. The beat is clarity: she has been choosing safety, not love.

chapters.title: The Sentence
chapters.summary: Climax, alternating POV. At the wedding, Vesper reads the exposed ledgers aloud instead of her vows as Elias delivers the council documents to the state attorney in the back pew. Aldous's allies scatter. Outside, in the rain, Elias finally says the sentence he rehearsed for a decade — and Vesper answers it with her own. The beat is rupture and release.

chapters.title: Signed
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV, epilogue-like. Spring: the orchard blooms again, the bookshop hosts its first open-mic, and Elias signs his name to a new letter — the only one he'll ever need to send, left on her pillow. Juniper calls them ridiculous. The beat is belonging, chosen freely at last.
